disclosure.title: Confidentiality & Disclosure Note
disclosure.text: I conducted the following four projects through Duke University collaborations from September 2023 to September 2026. Partner names and proprietary internal system identifiers are withheld under nondisclosure agreements. The collaborators include a leading multimodal foundation model developer, a frontier AI research laboratory, and a leading global alternative asset manager with more than $300 billion in assets under management. The project titles, my role as a researcher, locations, dates, system architectures, mathematical formulations, and reproducible synthetic benchmarks are cleared for public disclosure.

entries.organization: Duke University × Leading Foundation Model Developer
entries.summary: With a leading foundation model developer, I led the statistical system behind expert feedback for LLM post-training, one of the first engineering implementations of prediction-assisted statistical inference and capacity-constrained review allocation in expert data production. It coordinated more than 300 specialists and an external vendor network. Under ideal residual calibration, a synthetic benchmark showed 17.79% lower estimation variance than uniform sampling at equal audit cost.
entries.detailTitle: Large-Scale Domain Expert Feedback Governance and Adaptive Review

metadata.location: Durham, North Carolina; Palo Alto, California

keyContributions: **Starting in September 2023, I led the development of a collaboration system spanning more than 300 domain experts across several specialties.** Across the project's external expert and vendor networks, I defined the mathematical specifications and operating standards for task organization, reliability calibration, acceptance adjudication and review allocation. These procedures made distributed expert judgments traceable and subject to calibration as post-training feedback. This was among the first engineering implementations of prediction-assisted statistical inference and capacity-constrained review allocation in expert data production.

**I designed tiered review rules from Beta-Binomial reliability posteriors, credible intervals, verified sample counts and task-level risk priors.** In one workflow, a flagged submission was dynamically assigned to three additional specialists, and an initially accepted one went to one or two. The expert adjudications then fed back into the system, updating contributor reliability posteriors, informing targeted coaching and adjusting review intensity.

**I combined independent random reference audits with escalation of high-risk tasks to turn recurring annotator disagreements into explicit acceptance criteria.** I separated missing context from ambiguous instructions and from contributor errors, then revised the task instructions, boundary cases and shared calibration anchors accordingly. Later comparisons of Dawid-Skene reviewer-error models and cost-sensitive deferral rules (DeCCaF) informed the escalation thresholds.

**I built SQL and Python pipelines that brought together task metadata, review histories, acceptance outcomes, turnaround times and behavioral logs, and reconciled platform activity with Hubstaff operational telemetry.** The allocation solvers took their empirical estimates of unit verification costs ($c_i$), task-stratum latencies ($t_{iaj}$) and hard specialist capacity limits ($H_j^{\text{review}}$) from these records. I also translated client-reported model defects into reproducible engineering investigations and standard operating procedures.

**I formalized the production procedures by connecting prediction-assisted active statistical inference, cost-aware audit allocation and capacity-constrained review assignment.** For each task I defined an *initial error risk* ($q_i$), the *statistical information value of an independent reference audit* ($m_i / c_i$), and the *expected defect loss removable through additional human handling* ($\Delta_i = r_{i0} - r_{i1}$). I derived the sampling and review decisions that go with each quantity, which gave a reusable allocation method for expert feedback across domains.

**I tested the estimator and allocation algorithms on a stratified synthetic benchmark of 10,000 submissions, using 200,000 independent Monte Carlo sampling repetitions.** Under ideal residual calibration and an equal expected audit budget, allocating by residuals and costs cut population quality estimation variance by **17.79%** relative to uniform sampling, equivalent to a **9.33%** reduction in standard deviation. In a separate analytical example with 200 tasks, ranking reviews by marginal gain cut expected post-review defect loss by **8.89%** at the same review volume.

architecturalContext.title: Architectural Context: Statistical governance for expert data production
architecturalContext.text: When review succeeds in targeting the tasks with higher true error probabilities, the resulting selection bias is positive ($\operatorname{Cov}(\pi(X), q(X)) > 0$), so a raw inspection error rate has to be corrected before it can support population quality inference. Audit allocation has a related problem, since directing expert capacity toward the tasks that improve estimation precision means accounting for residual uncertainty and verification cost. The project's expert feedback governance framework for post-training had to deal with both across multiple domains. I began leading its development in September 2023. I coordinated hundreds of distributed specialists and external vendor queues and defined the mathematical specifications for quality measurement and resource allocation under selective review. The seven sections below formalize the production design and compare it with the methods literature, including references published from 2024 to 2026.

entries.organization: Duke University × Leading Foundation Model Developer
entries.summary: I designed the data strategy for financial post-training in a frontier foundation model program, one of the first engineering implementations of constraint-preserving synthetic data and structured expert preference supervision for financial LLM post-training. Diagnostic decision tasks, exact accounting constraints and a five-level preference protocol feed Batch Zero, the calibration protocol the company later extended to other post-training programs.
entries.detailTitle: Financial Task Design and Synthetic Data Engineering

metadata.location: Durham, North Carolina; Palo Alto, California

keyContributions: **Beginning in September 2023, I led financial and business decision task design for a frontier foundation model program, specifying the capability taxonomy, primary evidence standards, input schemas, decisive variables, and acceptance criteria.** The diagnostic cases targeted high-stakes business decision boundaries where foundation models and practitioners repeatedly make errors. They translated doctoral or CFA-level domain judgment into testable task requirements. Together with the synthesis methods and Batch Zero below, this work was among the first engineering implementations of constraint-preserving synthetic data and structured expert preference supervision for financial LLM post-training.

**I designed a five-level pairwise preference protocol for RLHF and DPO supervision.** It records why an expert prefers one response to another, and that record is how domain knowledge becomes post-training supervision. Each judgment has to cite verifiable evidence, the relevant accounting rules, and the decisive variables. The annotations keep the evidence and reasoning behind each preference and support training models to assess whether a financial judgment has sufficient support.

**I developed financial synthetic data methods for four settings.** For each task I selected a mathematical generator and adapted it to the task's structural invariants, data types, and permitted information:

**I created Batch Zero to implement post-training data strategy.** Starting from the capability objectives and data requirements of post-training research teams, I established a protocol for independent execution and expert calibration that a task family goes through before it enters large-scale data construction. Doctoral-level domain experts independently construct tasks, generate synthetic variants, solve reference cases, and assign five-level pairwise preference scores. The disagreements and failure modes that appear in execution inform revisions to task specifications, boundary cases, and **Batch One** data acceptance criteria. The foundation model company subsequently extended **Batch Zero** to other new post-training programs.

**I quantified stale-label errors, temporal leakage, and task-family clustering.** Analytical derivations and simulations show that when labels are not recomputed, synthetic perturbations near a decision boundary produce **40.13%** inherited-label error at $\gamma/s = 0.25$. Undisclosed Brownian bridge endpoint conditioning creates an apparent **29.29% reduction in RMSE** at the interval midpoint through future-information leakage. And with within-family correlation $\rho = 0.5$, 2,000 nominal synthetic variants from 100 task families amount to only **$N_{\text{eff}} \approx 190.48$** effective independent observations.

architecturalContext.title: Architectural Context: Task specifications and data strategy for financial post-training
architecturalContext.text:
In September 2023, frontier foundation models could reproduce corporate finance definitions and still made unpredictable errors in financial workflows, where a small numerical change or an accounting footnote could reverse an investment recommendation. I developed a data strategy around the capability objectives and data requirements of post-training research teams, connecting task specifications, synthesis methods, and expert calibration to address two problems:
1. **Diagnosing reasoning limits through task design.** I designed prompts around subtle business failure modes, including covenant breaches, off-balance-sheet adjustments, and valuation differences close to a decision boundary, because simple prompts may give little basis for telling candidate responses apart. Paired with the five-level preference protocol, these prompts turn a domain judgment such as *"Response A is better because it isolates the working-capital constraint and cites Footnote 4"* into structured preference supervision for post-training.
2. **Matching the generator to the financial structure.** Synthetic financial data has to satisfy structural constraints, stay consistent with reference judgments, and respect the task's information boundaries. A corporate table that violates Total Assets $=$ Total Liabilities $+$ Equity, even by a fraction of a percentage point, introduces a structural error. An interest-rate path that exposes a future terminal rate to a historical forecasting task introduces temporal leakage. Sections 1 through 6 give the conditions, analytical results, and validation designs for each method. Batch Zero then turns these requirements into acceptance criteria, under which experts have to be able to execute the task specification independently, reproduce reference solutions, and calibrate their judgments.

items: *Cross-sectional corporate fundamentals.* I used Gaussian and vine copulas with conditional sampling for company size, operating history, and financial ratios. These methods preserve joint dependencies across columns and avoid the unrealistic combinations that sampling each column independently produces.

*Accounting identities, ratio bounds, and chronological order.* Constrained sampling, variable transformations, and covariance-weighted affine projections enforce balance-sheet and cash-flow identities, ratio ranges, and date ordering. Across 200,000 12-dimensional synthetic draws, the maximum constraint residual was **$1.21 \times 10^{-14}$**. A separate standardized-residual rejection model had an acceptance rate of $0.0002529\%$.

*Multimodal records with numerical and categorical fields.* CTGAN and TabDDPM model the multimodal empirical distributions. Business-rule checks are mandatory after generation, and together with Lipschitz decision-margin tests and Gaussian margin-to-noise analysis ($\gamma/s$) they guide reference-answer recomputation and reduce stale supervision labels.

*Continuous-time price and interest-rate paths.* SDEs, neural SDEs, Brownian bridges, and stochastic interpolation generate paths for temporal financial tasks, while static cross-sectional company comparisons do not require these constructions. The work extends MathWorks-style stochastic interest-rate path construction and matches each method to the task's permitted filtration ($\mathcal{F}_s$), to keep future information from leaking into evaluation.

entries.organization: Duke University × Frontier AI Research Laboratory
entries.summary: I developed a framework for evaluating and supervising general reasoning with a frontier AI research laboratory, among the first engineering implementations of joint verification across final answers, visible reasoning and execution evidence in frontier model evaluation. Code checks, LLM-as-a-Judge screening and specialist scholars work in three layers. On 3,600 benchmark submissions, certificate checking made no false acceptances, where final-answer matching falsely accepted 75.0%.
entries.detailTitle: General Reasoning Evaluation and Layered Verification

metadata.location: Durham, North Carolina; Palo Alto, California

keyContributions: **I developed a joint evaluation method for answers, visible reasoning, and execution evidence.** Beginning in September 2023, I brought the model's displayed CoT, its actual tool calls and its intermediate outputs into the review workflow. I assessed the validity of conclusions, compliance with task requirements and progress during problem solving as separate dimensions. This was among the first engineering implementations of joint verification across final answers, visible reasoning and execution evidence in frontier model evaluation.

**I organized deliverables into proof-obligation dependency graphs ($\Gamma_q \vdash C_q$).** The graphs track domain assumptions, method applicability, evidentiary support, compliant execution, uniform approximation bounds and the strength of each conclusion. They help me locate the first unsupported step and what it affects downstream, and they allow valid alternative derivations. For tasks that admit formalization, checking local nodes and their dependencies within a sound inference system establishes the full conclusion.

**I developed checkable error certificates and bounds on solution quality for programmatically verifiable task families under explicit mathematical assumptions.** The projected-residual optimality bound ($0 \le f(x) - v^* \le \|P_{\ker A} r\|_2^2 / (2\mu)$) splits feasibility, stationarity and the accuracy of a conclusion into separate verification obligations, and different proofs can pass by satisfying the same ones. Section 3 gives the assumptions, certificate construction and problem class.

**I established a division of work among code or rule checks, LLM-assisted screening, and review by scholars with relevant expertise.** Code checks directly verifiable answers, tool permissions and other requirements specified in advance. LLM-as-a-Judge helps flag missing evidence, misapplied rules and gaps in reasoning, and disputed domain judgments go to specialist scholars. I also compare elapsed time, attempt counts, changes in intermediate outputs and the use of tool results to find redundant work and loops without progress, keeping those efficiency findings apart from correctness judgments.

**I derived how false acceptance ($\alpha$) and false rejection ($\beta$) can reverse model rankings and bias the binary cross-entropy gradient used to train process reward models ($E[\nabla_s \ell(s,V) - \nabla_s \ell(s,Z) \mid h] = p(h) - \tilde{p}(h)$).** I also derived the exact tolerance-propagation rule ($a\delta + 2\varepsilon$) for bijective task transformations. Between them, these results specify when grading labels and transformed tasks support valid comparisons.

**I tested false acceptance and false rejection on 3,600 exact-arithmetic submissions from 600 constructed strongly convex quadratic task families.** In this benchmark, 75% of invalid proofs reported the correct final value. Certificate checking accepted all 1,200 valid proofs (0.0% false rejection) and rejected all 2,400 invalid submissions (0.0% false acceptance). Final-answer matching had a 75.0% false acceptance rate and strict reference-path matching a 50.0% false rejection rate. The constructed families, defined in Section 6, test both error detection and the retention of valid alternative proofs.

architecturalContext.title: Architectural Context: Visible reasoning and execution evidence
architecturalContext.text: The collaboration began in fall 2023 with an evaluation of general reasoning in frontier models. In my workflow a correct answer could coexist with unsupported assumptions, misapplied rules, or tool use that violated the task specification. Repeated calls that left the evidence and intermediate results unchanged exposed opportunities to improve execution as well. So I cross-checked final answers, the model's visible reasoning, execution records and efficiency measures, and divided the responsibilities among programmatic checks, LLM-assisted semantic screening and review by specialist scholars. The project ran to September 2026. Sections 1 through 7 describe the acceptance criteria, the mathematical certificates for a programmatically verifiable subfamily, and the associated experiments, and compare them with the methods literature, including papers published during the project.

items: I cross-check the displayed CoT against actual tool calls, return values and intermediate outputs to see whether what the model claims in its reasoning has observable support.
Code or rules check directly verifiable answers, required deliverables, and approved tools and execution environments, with compliance judged against the requirements specified for the task.

From elapsed time, attempt counts and changes in intermediate results I identify repeated operations, continued use of failed assumptions and attempts that add no evidence. These findings inform efficiency analysis even when the final answer is correct, and any resource limit used to determine acceptance has to be defined in the task specification beforehand.

entries.organization: Duke University × Leading Global Alternative Asset Manager
entries.summary: I developed and implemented a framework for evidence verification and decision assurance with a leading global alternative asset manager, one of the first engineering implementations in institutional investment research to treat model multiplicity, unverified evidence and the cost of verification jointly. It tells analysts which fact to verify next: in an eight-scenario benchmark, one targeted query cut worst-case regret from 0.61 score units to zero.
entries.detailTitle: Evidence Verification and Robust Comparison in Investment Research
keyContributions: **I studied what AI-polished corporate narratives do to LLM-assisted scoring, ESG ratings and investment analysis when the claims underneath them lack factual support.** I brought corporate claims, cross-document contradictions and shared reporting errors into a common review process so that verification in private-market and ESG research could be targeted.

**I turned institutional diligence requirements into measures of score reliability, pairwise ranking stability and verification priority.** The workflow I implemented ingests evidence, scores companies across a Rashomon model set, computes ranking bounds, and allocates verification effort by minimax regret. Each correction triggers rescoring and attribution updates, so the investment committee has a traceable basis for its analysis. This was among the first engineering implementations in institutional investment research to treat model multiplicity, unverified evidence and the cost of verification jointly.

**I converted operating reports, audited financial statements, sustainability disclosures, management questionnaires and third-party datasets into structured scoring rules that carry source and version records.** AI-assisted checks then pick out unsupported claims and contradictions across documents for targeted factual review.

**I deployed gradient-boosted trees and deep learning models for tabular data to capture nonlinear thresholds and interactions.** SHAP attributions across a near-optimal Rashomon set ($\mathcal{F}_\alpha$), read together with conditional Shapley analysis, measure sensitivity to model choice and identify the scoring factors whose contributions stay stable across models.

**I derived failure cases for conventional bootstrap resampling, and for verification priorities based on raw SHAP magnitudes, when inputs contain shared reporting bias or unverified claims.** I represented unresolved evidence $\mathcal{X}(E)$ jointly with the Rashomon set $\mathcal{F}_\alpha$ through $\Omega(E) = \mathcal{F}_\alpha \times \mathcal{X}(E)$ and derived convex support-function bounds ($h_U(a_f)$). Common measurement errors cancel when the two companies have identical exposures. In a synthetic comparison, the joint model certified a 0.6-point advantage that the difference bound from separate company intervals ($[-1.4, 2.6]$) could not show.

**I derived a query criterion that needs no probability distribution over the scenarios inside the specified joint uncertainty set.** It prioritizes the reduction in worst-case decision regret that a query can guarantee. For unequal query costs, $V(q)/c_q$ gives a one-step efficiency measure. In an eight-scenario benchmark with one equal-cost query, targeted verification cut worst-case regret from 0.61 score units to zero, whereas rechecking an already verified feature with a large SHAP attribution reduced regret by zero.

architecturalContext.title: Architectural Context: Corporate evidence and the allocation of verification effort
architecturalContext.text: AI-polished narratives, unverified sustainability claims and common reporting errors can all move ESG and investment scores, so institutional diligence has to account for uncertainty in the corporate evidence as well as in the scoring models. The architecture I developed takes a traceable evidence state as its input and builds in model multiplicity, joint measurement error and the costs of verification. Sections 1 through 6 go through the limits of attribution methods, the joint uncertainty model, ranking bounds, the query criterion, versioned updates, and analytical benchmarks.

entries.summary: Owned business development for Jiritsu's asset-verification and privacy-preserving computation services as the sole dedicated contributor for new issuers. Reported directly to a co-founder, combining data engineering, preference ranking, and counterparty discussions to develop partnership recommendations for the board.
keyContributions: Served as the sole dedicated contributor to business development for new issuers, reporting to co-founder Asher Gottesman. Turned commercialization priorities into screening criteria, experiments, data requirements, and outreach plans; independently managed analysis, counterparty discussions, and recommendations.

Organized core-team reviews with commercial input from Asher Gottesman and technical and financial guidance from Gene Itkis of MIT Lincoln Laboratory and Michael Lustig, former Senior Managing Director at BlackRock and Adjunct Professor of Finance at NYU Stern. Assessed applied cryptography, zero-knowledge applications, technical fit, liquidity, and risk.

Designed a two-stage framework for real-world assets, stablecoins, DeFi, and infrastructure: test identity, liquidity, pricing validity, data completeness, and risk, then rank commercial fit and accessibility. Used issuer-level error analysis to refine qualification rules, exclude out-of-scope projects, and record evidence-backed reasons for each decision.

Resolved issuer identities across CoinGecko, chain records, websites, white papers, and disclosures. Reconciled multichain listings and wrapped or bridged assets to remove duplicate opportunities. Built market and text features spanning liquidity, capitalization, activity, project age, chain affiliation, business models, and technical needs.

Built a Python, Prefect, DuckDB, and Parquet pipeline for ingestion, standardization, entity mapping, feature preparation, and querying. Implemented scheduled refreshes, retries, persisted outputs, reruns, and historical backfills to support model training and repeatable shortlist updates.

Trained a LightGBM pairwise ranking model on the core team's comparisons of eligible counterparties. Combined commercial, disclosure, and market features to prioritize approximately 800 potential partners. Repeated comparison, retraining, and ranking over two to four weeks, using uncertainty sampling to focus expert review on borderline candidates, near ties, and conflicting evidence.

Applied issuer similarity analysis and Leiden community detection to discover overlooked projects with related business or technical characteristics, then brought qualified candidates into commercial review and ranking.

Led Codex-assisted solution design and Python development. Used meta prompting and ChatGPT deep research to translate business objectives into analytical plans and development specifications; selected methods, debugged workflows, and verified issuer-level outputs and selection rationales.

Screened 18,000+ token records into approximately 800 potential counterparties, 30 outreach priorities, and six proposed pilot counterparties. Discussed asset-verification needs, service arrangements, and technology licensing with prospects, and delivered the candidate list and commercial assessments to the board for technical and business evaluation.

entries.summary: Led the China workstream of a global market-entry engagement covering China, Japan, and the Middle East for a premium European appliance brand. Combined market data, consumer evidence, and policy research to recommend local products, pricing, channels, and marketing while maintaining the client's global positioning.
entries.detailTitle: China Market Entry for a Premium European Appliance Brand
keyContributions: Built a MECE analytical framework spanning product fit, pricing, channels, marketing, and policy. Defined which elements of the client's premium positioning should remain consistent globally and where the China strategy required local adaptation.

Specified data requirements across five e-commerce platforms and seven appliance categories, coordinating with data scientists on collection and local analysts on validation. Owned downstream processing and interpretation of approximately 50,000 listings in Python, standardizing attributes, efficiency labels, prices, promotions, and reviews while preserving channel-specific observations.

Mapped competitors in Tableau by category, price band, efficiency, and features. Combined product comparisons with consumer reviews to identify relatively underserved segments, including high-efficiency products at mid- to high-price points, and assessed opportunities in tier-1 and tier-2 cities.

Evaluated the European portfolio against Chinese usage needs, product dimensions, and efficiency requirements. Recommended local assortments and compared the brand's website, e-commerce, physical retail, and channel partnerships, incorporating Xiaohongshu and Douyin into marketing analysis.

Researched efficiency standards, subsidies, certification, and market access through published sources and expert interviews, including think-tank discussions. Built entry scenarios by category and city tier, translating current requirements and expected policy changes into product-introduction and timing recommendations.

Delivered the China market report and represented the workstream in global project meetings. Presented the evidence behind product, pricing, channel, and marketing recommendations; coordinated green-product definitions and policy assumptions. Documented field mappings and processing rules in a reusable template for subsequent regional analysis.
Received a full-time offer from Euromonitor's consulting team during the internship.

entries.summary: Applied statistical methods to sustainability assessment and green-credit screening within China Construction Bank's internal framework. Combined company data, historical assessments, and explicit eligibility rules to support candidate review, then documented the method for product managers and risk officers evaluating its use on a platform.
entries.detailTitle: PCA-Based Sustainability Analysis and Green-Credit Screening
keyContributions: Analyzed financial, operational, and environmental data for approximately 2,000 entities within CCB's framework of more than 30 indicators, assessing overall scores alongside minimum requirements for individual metrics.

Used PCA to identify overlapping indicator information and construct compact representations for candidate comparison. Applied supervised learning to historically labeled cases, examining feature patterns associated with positive and negative assessments and adding empirical evidence to candidate assessment.
Incorporated life cycle assessment principles into sustainability analysis, examining operating and environmental factors alongside financial performance.
Tested the initial top 30% of ranked candidates against individual-metric and overall-score minimums, retaining approximately 28% of the full pool for further research and review.

Reviewed selection and exclusion patterns across the pool, separating ranking cutoffs from threshold failures. Converted borderline cases, unmet requirements, and follow-up questions into a reusable checklist linked to the applicable screening rules.
Delivered a methodology note explaining scoring logic, data sources, model behavior, and edge cases to product managers and risk officers assessing the method for platform use.

entries.organization: Autonomous Authority in Space: Risk Tradeoffs and the Law of Delegation
entries.summary: I developed a legal framework for authorizing autonomous space operations when delayed human intervention creates risks of its own. I formulated a two-threshold test separating the authority to act from the evidence needed to delegate execution, applied it to delayed spacecraft operations, orbital avoidance, debris capture, and SETI, and proposed task-specific authorization records. The resulting framework identifies which decisions can be authorized in advance, which require renewed review, and what evidence must support each choice.
entries.detailTitle: Autonomous Authority in Space: Risk Tradeoffs and the Law of Delegation
keyContributions: Specified a two-threshold decision procedure linking legal authority, evidence for delegation, and the time at which human review can still change the outcome. Distinguished individual approval, advance-constrained action, and fallback behavior as separate supervisory choices.

Designed a task-specific authorization record specifying responsible actors, permitted actions, operating conditions, exposed interests, and reassessment triggers. Connected these terms to independent scrutiny and event records that allow consequential decisions to be reconstructed.

Compared delayed spacecraft operations and orbital avoidance against existing automation and ground review. Analyzed how latency, uncertain trajectories, simultaneous maneuvers, and failed coordination affect delegation and redistribute risk among operators.

Used debris capture and SETI to distinguish technical capability from permission to affect another party's interests or confirm a scientific interpretation. Proposed scientific verification through alternative explanations, independent observations, and documented evidence.

Integrated review delays, compliance costs, disclosure risks, and correlated failures into the proposed controls. Developed proportionate reassessment around material changes, reusable evidence, and legally competent institutions, making the burdens of supervision part of the authorization decision.

entries.organization: Small States and the Governance of Strategic Space Dependence
entries.summary: I developed a comparative legal framework for assessing small states' control over foreign-dependent space infrastructure. I analyzed New Zealand's launch regulation, Norway's Arctic satellite partnership, and Luxembourg's LUXEOSys procurement to distinguish permission, ownership, operational rights, and implementation capacity. I proposed an accountable-acceptance standard for strategic dependencies, linking interruption powers and response rights to funded capability. The analysis identifies specific institutional remedies for licensing, service continuity, procurement oversight, and collective action.
entries.detailTitle: Small States and the Governance of Strategic Space Dependence
keyContributions: Built a structured comparison around specific public functions and the decisions needed to perform them, defining practical autonomy as the capacity to make and implement a specified lawful public decision. Examined external dependencies, legal and operational rights, domestic capability, and documented outcomes to assess whether retained authority could support an actual public decision.

Identified distinct mechanisms in the three cases: retained launch-permission authority in New Zealand, operational capability through divided responsibilities in Norway, and the planning and legislative information required alongside asset ownership in Luxembourg.

Proposed an accountable-acceptance standard requiring decision makers to identify who can interrupt essential services, which information and rights permit a response, and what funded capacity enables action. Material gaps would require reasoned acceptance or revision before commitment.

Translated the standard into proposed licensing and procurement terms covering operator information, significant changes, suspension, recovery, and service transition. Connected these terms to lifetime costs, technical staffing, and timely legislative scrutiny of financial commitments.

Analyzed collective agency through anti-satellite-testing commitments, UN consensus procedures, and ESA programme and voting rules. Distinguished participation rights, influence, and implementation capacity, connecting national safeguards to collective restraint on debris and cross-border service disruption.

entries.organization: Who May Choose the Lesser Risk: Solar Geoengineering and the Legal Duties of Comparison and Continuity
entries.summary: I proposed and developed two legal duties for solar geoengineering: comparative justification and continuity. The first connects risk-risk analysis to authorization by requiring proponents to defend policy alternatives and answer challenges from affected constituencies. For the second, I traced termination risk to a separation between political control, operator succession, and the physical cooling trajectory. The resulting framework specifies conditions for deployment and withdrawal, supports governed research, and requires continuing assessment of both intervention and nondeployment.
entries.detailTitle: Who May Choose the Lesser Risk: Solar Geoengineering and the Legal Duties of Comparison and Continuity
keyContributions: Separated historical climate conditions, a future without stratospheric aerosol injection, and feasible policy portfolios as distinct comparators. Analyzed how baseline selection, welfare measures, and distributional assumptions shape the case for intervention and the burdens assigned to exposed populations.

Proposed a comparative justification duty requiring proponents to defend alternatives, disclose distributional choices, and answer substantiated objections. Designed powers for independently selected representatives of exposed constituencies to demand redesign or withhold collective approval.

Developed a continuity duty separating program control, operator choice, and the cooling trajectory. Specified bounded interim succession, independent monitoring, transition finance, and gradual withdrawal so that political authority can change without automatically triggering abrupt physical cessation.

Mapped environmental assessment, notification, and consultation requirements onto the authorization problem. Distinguished limited research from climate-affecting deployment and proposed scrutiny based on expected effects and cumulative scale, including review of related projects together.

Formulated a priority rule for serious threats to subsistence and survival, requiring comparison of feasible alternatives, shared authorization, and credible relief. Built periodic reassessment of forgone benefits and harms of nondeployment into the same decision process.

entries.organization: Mangrove Restoration and the Limits of Compensatory Mitigation: Lessons from Florida for the Greater Bay Area
entries.summary: I developed a comparative legal framework for deciding when ecological restoration can justify new habitat loss. It distinguishes protection, repair, and compensatory mitigation across Florida and the Greater Bay Area, and it uses West Lake, Deep Bay, and San Tin to examine evidence of functional replacement. I proposed site-specific baselines, staged authorization and ecological acceptance, funded correction, and continuing responsibility. The framework connects restoration evidence to development permissions, funding decisions, and the point at which obligations can be discharged.
entries.detailTitle: Mangrove Restoration and the Limits of Compensatory Mitigation: Lessons from Florida for the Greater Bay Area
keyContributions: Organized the legal comparison around habitat protection, repair, and compensation for new loss. Traced duties, approval instruments, and administrative powers across Florida, mainland China, Shenzhen, Hong Kong, and Macao to identify how restoration conditions can take legal effect.

Used West Lake to examine hydrological rehabilitation and Deep Bay and San Tin to assess functional replacement. Distinguished canopy growth, construction, and predicted enhancement from evidence supporting compensation, including additionality and the timing of replacement functions.

Proposed staged approval and acceptance separating engineering completion from ecological performance. Specified site baselines, functional objectives, monitoring periods, seasonal coverage, and review authority, linking damaging development phases to the availability of the functions used to justify them.

Designed arrangements for delayed or failed recovery through funded monitoring, correction, and continuing management. Distinguished contractor performance from ecological uncertainty, and examined retention, financial security, and public budget commitments as instruments for sustaining corrective work.

Linked ecological evidence to fund release, discharge of responsibility, and development permission. Proposed smaller footprints, revised sequencing, alternative sites, or refusal to credit compensation where promised functions lack credible replacement, while allowing proportionate trials in degraded habitats.

entries.organization: Jones Lang LaSalle Capital Markets Team
entries.summary: Served as the project team's ESG lead on acquisition advisory for a Southeast Asian conglomerate seeking Chinese office properties. Worked with JLL's internal ESG team to connect asset screening, property valuation, and site-level diligence with the client's investment requirements and potential refurbishment or repositioning plans.
entries.detailTitle: Office Investment Underwriting and ESG Due Diligence
keyContributions: Screened 22 cities across four investable regions against client preferences, preliminary budgets, market liquidity, and institutional-grade office stock. Narrowed the search to 20 assets in Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Shenzhen, and Chengdu.

Developed a GRESB-informed desktop screen with approximately 40 ESG and operating indicators, coordinating with JLL's internal ESG team. Flagged environmental, operating, and capital-expenditure concerns that excluded approximately 40% of candidates before full valuation and due diligence.

Structured diligence across management, performance, and development: ownership and SPV transparency, policy coverage, compliance, safety, and 12 months of continuous operating records. Benchmarked energy, carbon, water, waste, certifications, and upgrades against comparable properties matched by city, submarket, vintage, and building systems.

Assessed upgrade, refurbishment, and extension risks through capital-expenditure and cash-flow analysis. Used equipment age, chiller efficiency, building-management systems, sub-metering, air monitoring, and maintenance records as proxies where utility data were unavailable. Converted findings into red, amber, and green signals and asset-specific diligence priorities.

Underwrote shortlisted properties using discounted cash flow, replacement cost, and comparable transactions, incorporating operating conditions and upgrade requirements into valuation assumptions, cash-flow scenarios, and exit-risk assessments.
Built ten dashboards in Excel, Python, and Tableau to compare market fundamentals, valuations, ESG indicators, and scenario exposures across cities, assets, and the investment pipeline.

Led bilingual briefings for capital-markets leadership and client managers, shaped site-visit sequencing and ESG questions, and delivered standardized asset books covering tenant concentration, weighted average lease expiry, vacancy, rents, operating costs, valuation models, and diligence findings.

entries.summary: Led shipping, logistics, and industrial asset-tracking research for Hubble's Bluetooth satellite commercialization through a Duke Practicum. Assessed where the technology's cost, accuracy, power consumption, and periodic reporting capabilities matched customer needs, translating technical and market evidence into recommendations for early applications.
entries.detailTitle: Bluetooth Satellite Commercialization and Market Selection

metadata.position: Student Consultant and Business Analytics Analyst, Duke Practicum

keyContributions: Led the shipping, logistics, and industrial tracking workstreams after Hubble's $20 million Series A and before its first satellite launches.
